ap_physics_c_mechanics-f01.title: Block hanging from a pulley with rotational inertia

stimulus.description: A block of mass $m=3\text{ kg}$ hangs from a light string that is wrapped around a pulley. The pulley is a uniform disk of mass $M=2\text{ kg}$ and radius $R=0.1\text{ m}$ and can rotate about a fixed, frictionless horizontal axle through its center; its rotational inertia is $\tfrac12MR^2$. The string does not slip on the pulley. The block is released from rest. Use $g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the dot below, which represents the hanging block, draw and label the forces (not components) that act on the block while it falls. Each force must be represented by a distinct arrow starting on the dot.
parts.model_answer: Two arrows from the dot: weight straight down and tension straight up; the weight arrow is longer than the tension arrow because the block accelerates downward.

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws and labels the weight (down) and the tension (up), with no extra force such as a force of motion
common_errors: adds a force of motion downward

rubric_rows.criterion: The directions are correct: weight straight down and tension straight up
common_errors: draws the tension downward

rubric_rows.criterion: The weight arrow is longer than the tension arrow because the block accelerates downward
common_errors: draws equal lengths for an accelerating block

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the magnitude $a$ of the acceleration of the block in terms of $m$, $M$ and $g$.
parts.model_answer: $mg-T=ma$ for the block and $TR=(\tfrac12MR^2)(a/R)$ for the pulley give $T=\tfrac12Ma$, so $a=mg/(m+M/2)$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies Newton's second law to the block: $mg-T=ma$
common_errors: uses T = m g

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies the rotational form of Newton's second law to the pulley with $a=\alpha R$: $TR=\tfrac12MR^2(a/R)$, so $T=\tfrac12Ma$
common_errors: omits the rotational inertia of the pulley

rubric_rows.criterion: Combines the equations to $a=mg/(m+M/2)$
common_errors: obtains $mg/(m+M)$

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the acceleration of the block for $m=3\text{ kg}$ and $M=2\text{ kg}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Substitutes the values into the expression from part B
common_errors: uses the full mass of the pulley, $M$, in place of $M/2$

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains about 7.35 with units of meters per second squared

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The pulley is replaced by a uniform disk of the same radius but twice the mass. Does the magnitude of the acceleration of the block increase, decrease, or stay the same? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: It decreases, because a pulley with twice the mass has twice the rotational inertia, so $a=mg/(m+M/2)$ has a larger denominator.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the acceleration decreases
common_errors: states that the acceleration is unchanged because the hanging mass is unchanged

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the larger pulley mass increases the effective inertia ($m+M/2$) of the system, or that more of the energy goes into rotation
common_errors: argues only that the pulley is heavier

parts.model_answer: Agree. For a circular orbit $K=GMm/(2r)$ decreases as $r$ increases, while $E=K+U=-GMm/(2r)$ is negative and becomes less negative (increases) as $r$ increases.

rubric_rows.criterion: Agrees with the claim
common_errors: disagrees because a higher orbit has more energy in every form

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies the decrease of the kinetic energy with $K=GMm/(2r)$ from the centripetal condition
common_errors: says the kinetic energy increases with the height

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies the increase of the total energy with $E=-GMm/(2r)$, which becomes less negative as $r$ increases
common_errors: says the total energy is positive

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the total mechanical energy of the satellite in a circular orbit of radius $r$, and calculate the change in the total mechanical energy when the satellite moves from $r_1$ to $r_2$.
parts.model_answer: $GMm/r^2=mv^2/r$ gives $K=GMm/(2r)$, and $E=K+U=-GMm/(2r)$. $\Delta E=\tfrac12GMm(1/r_1-1/r_2)\approx6.23e+09\text{ J}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Sets the gravitational force equal to the centripetal force to get $K=GMm/(2r)$
required_elements: G M m / r^2 = m v^2 / r
common_errors: uses K = G M m / r

rubric_rows.criterion: Adds the potential energy $U=-GMm/r$ to obtain $E=-GMm/(2r)$
required_elements: E = K + U = - G M m / (2 r)
common_errors: obtains $E=+GMm/(2r)$

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $\Delta E=\tfrac12GMm(1/r_1-1/r_2)$ of about 6.23e+09 with units of joules (positive)
common_errors: gives a negative change

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Predict the ratio of the orbital speed in the larger orbit to the orbital speed in the original orbit, and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The ratio is $v_2/v_1=\sqrt{r_1/r_2}=1/\sqrt{2}\approx0.707$, because $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the speed ratio is about 0.707 (the speed decreases)
common_errors: states that the speed increases
states a ratio of 0.500

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$, so the speed is inversely proportional to the square root of the radius
common_errors: argues only that the satellite is farther away
